analysis.one_liner: Cuts taxes for working families, repeals the individual minimum tax, and taxes fund managers' carried interest as ordinary income.
analysis.headline: The bill got no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors; it died in the Ways and Means Committee when the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill from the chairman of the tax-writing committee would have cut taxes for low- and moderate-income workers, families with children, and the roughly 20 million households who pay the alternative minimum tax. To pay for it, it would raise taxes on people making over $250,000, tax hedge fund and private equity managers' 'carried interest' as regular salary income instead of low-taxed capital gains, close several corporate accounting shelters, and lower the top corporate rate from 35% to 30.5%. It never received a single committee action after being referred.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income workers gain from a bigger standard deduction and a doubled earned income credit rate for workers without children (7.65% to 15.3%). Families with children gain because the refundable child credit starts phasing in at $8,500 of earnings instead of $10,000. Households hit by the alternative minimum tax — many of them middle- and upper-middle-income families in high-tax states — would see that tax repealed after 2007. Investors would gain from brokers being required to report the cost basis of securities, making tax filing simpler.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers without children, families, AMT payers

how_it_helps.text: The earned income credit rate for workers with no qualifying children would double from 7.65% to 15.3%, and the phaseout range would more than double, directly increasing take-home pay for the lowest-earning workers.
The refundable child credit would begin phasing in at $8,500 of earnings rather than $10,000, extending the credit to more low-income families.

The bill would repeal the individual alternative minimum tax after 2007, replacing the revenue with a surtax on incomes above roughly $200,000-$250,000 and new limits on itemized deductions and personal exemptions for incomes over $250,000.

Investment managers' carried interest — partnership income for managing other people's money — would be taxed as ordinary income for services performed, closing a tax break that let fund managers pay capital gains rates on their pay.
Brokers would have to report customers' cost basis on securities sales, reducing the burden and error rate for ordinary taxpayers computing capital gains.

analysis.who_pays: Individuals with adjusted gross income over $250,000 would lose deductions and pay a new surtax. Hedge fund, private equity, and real estate investment managers would pay ordinary income rates on carried interest, with a 40% penalty for avoidance. Corporations would lose the domestic production deduction, LIFO inventory accounting, and several foreign-income rules, though the top corporate rate would drop from 35% to 30.5%. Brokers and fund companies would bear new reporting compliance costs.

drawbacks.text: The bill lowers the top corporate rate to 30.5% even while closing shelters, so corporations as a class would pay less in total tax even as individuals' code is reformed; critics of the proposal argued this shift benefited shareholders and executives.

Repealing LIFO and lower-of-cost-or-market inventory accounting and shortening the domestic production deduction would raise bookkeeping complexity and taxes for manufacturers and energy firms, costs that could be passed to consumers.

Imposing self-employment taxes on service-providing S corporation shareholders and partners would raise taxes on many small professional practices, which objected that the rule could not distinguish passive owners from working owners.

The bill gives almost nothing to middle-income itemizers in high-tax states other than AMT repeal, and the new surtax design would leave many of the same households that the AMT hits paying an alternative tax instead of eliminating the problem.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core bargain is honest and clearly drawn: meaningful tax cuts for low-income workers and families, funded by taxing carried interest as compensation and limiting deductions above $250,000. The corporate rate cut is the weakest part — it lowers the headline rate faster than the loophole closures pay for it, and some of the offsetting provisions (LIFO repeal, self-employment tax expansion) would raise real compliance and cost burdens for businesses. But on net the bill's design moves the tax code toward taxing service income and high incomes rather than work and wages.

outcome.mechanism: Rangel, who chaired the very committee the bill was sent to, never scheduled a markup or floor vote, and it sat in the Ways and Means Committee until the 110th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Charles Rangel, chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, introduced the bill on October 25, 2007.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day it was introduced, and the action history shows no further action of any kind: no hearing, no markup, no vote.
No member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.

The bill carried provisions — carried interest taxation, LIFO repeal, and a surtax on high incomes — that were the target of intense opposition from the financial and investment management industry during 2007-2008.
The Congress ended January 3, 2009, with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Investment fund managers and corporations were better off because the bill died: carried interest stayed taxed at capital gains rates, the corporate rate stayed at 35%, and high earners avoided the new surtax and deduction limits. Congress continued the annual pattern of patching the AMT instead of repealing it.

for.name: Rep. Charles Rangel
for.role: Chairman, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it on October 25, 2007, as the committee chairman's own tax reform proposal.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.role: Tax-writing committee that received the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on October 25, 2007, and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, and no vote for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Private equity and hedge fund managers
against.role: Investment industry targeted by the carried interest provision
against.what_they_did: Lobbied heavily against taxing carried interest as ordinary income during the 2007 debate, contributing to the bill going nowhere despite its sponsor chairing the tax committee.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no colleague cosponsored, so the record shows no partisan breakdown — only a Democratic chairman's bill that drew no cosponsors from either party.

industries.industry: Private equity, hedge funds, and real estate investment managers
industries.note: The bill would tax their carried interest — their main source of pay — as ordinary income at rates up to 35% instead of 15% capital gains rates, with a 40% penalty for avoidance schemes. This is the industry the bill most directly targeted.

The top corporate rate would fall from 35% to 30.5%, but the domestic production deduction, LIFO accounting, and several foreign-income rules would be repealed, and the corporate AMT would remain. The net rate cut is a transfer toward corporations even as shelters close.

industries.industry: Accounting and tax compliance services (brokers, mutual funds, CPAs)
industries.note: Broker basis reporting would shift compliance work onto financial firms but make capital gains reporting far easier for ordinary taxpayers, who currently reconstruct basis by hand.

industries.industry: Small service businesses organized as S corporations and partnerships
industries.note: Service-providing owners would have to pay self-employment taxes on their share of business income, raising costs for law firms, doctors' practices, and consultancies.
